title: Antibiotics and the 1900s
bigQuestion: How did new discoveries and public health work help people in the 1900s live much longer lives?

story.title: The Moldy Dish
story.kicker: A scientist comes home from vacation and notices what is not growing.
paragraphs: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming came back to his lab at St. Mary's Hospital in London after a summer vacation. Fleming studied bacteria. Before he left, he had stacked glass dishes of bacteria on his bench. Now he began sorting them to clean up.

One dish looked spoiled. A fuzzy blue-green mold had grown on it. Many scientists would have tossed it out. But Fleming looked closer. All around the mold was a clear ring. The bacteria that covered the rest of the dish had not grown there.

Something from the mold was stopping the bacteria. Fleming grew more of the mold, a kind of Penicillium, and tested the juice it made. It stopped many kinds of harmful bacteria. He named the substance penicillin and reported it in 1929.

Fleming could not make enough pure penicillin to treat patients. That took another team more than ten years, and a war, and help from a lab in Peoria, Illinois. But it all began because one scientist noticed a clear ring on a dish that looked like a mistake.
story.think: Fleming noticed what was not there. Why can an unexpected result be as useful as an expected one?

sections.title: New Ways to See and Treat

lessons.title: X-Rays Show the Inside
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays, which let doctors see bones inside the body without surgery.
reading: In November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen was testing electric current in a glass tube in a darkened room. He noticed that a screen across the room began to glow. Some unknown ray was passing through the air, and even through paper and wood. He called it the X-ray, because X stands for something unknown.

Röntgen found that the rays passed through skin and muscle but were blocked by bone. He made an image of his wife's hand that showed her bones and her ring. Within months, doctors around the world were using *X-rays* to find broken bones and swallowed objects.

Early users did not know that strong doses of X-rays could harm the body. Some workers were hurt. Today *radiology* uses much smaller doses, and staff wear shields. Röntgen won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. X-rays opened the door to later imaging such as CT scans.

words.d: invisible rays that pass through soft tissue but are blocked by bone, used to make pictures of the inside of the body
the branch of medicine that uses images such as X-rays to find and treat problems

look.title: A Picture Without a Cut
look.text: A girl falls off her bike and her wrist swells. Before 1895, a doctor could only feel the wrist and guess. Now a technician places her hand on a plate, steps behind a shield and takes an image. The doctor sees a thin crack in one bone.
look.prompt: How does seeing the crack change what the doctor can do? What did doctors have to do before X-rays?

check.q: Why did Röntgen call his discovery the X-ray?
choices: It was shaped like an X
It came from a star named X
check.why: Röntgen used X, the sign for an unknown, because he did not know what the rays were.

check.q: What part of the body blocks X-rays and shows up clearly?
check.why: X-rays pass through skin and muscle but are blocked by bone.

check.q: Why do X-ray staff wear shields today?
choices: Strong doses of X-rays can harm the body
check.why: Early workers were hurt by strong doses, so today doses are small and staff use shields.

lessons.title: Insulin for Diabetes
lessons.mainIdea: In 1921–22, Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto helped discover insulin, which let people with type 1 diabetes live.
reading: Before the 1920s, a child with type 1 diabetes usually lived only a short time. In *diabetes*, the body cannot control the sugar in the blood. In type 1, the pancreas, an organ near the stomach, stops making enough of a hormone called *insulin*. Without insulin, the body cannot use sugar for energy.

In 1921, at the University of Toronto in Canada, Frederick Banting and his student helper Charles Best took insulin from the pancreas of dogs. Chemist James Collip helped purify it, in a lab led by John Macleod. In January 1922, a fourteen-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson received insulin and grew stronger.

Insulin does not cure diabetes. It is a treatment a person needs every day. But it turned a deadly illness into one people can live with for a long, full life. Today many people with diabetes check their blood sugar and take insulin with help from their doctor and care team.

words.d: a condition in which the body cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood
a hormone made by the pancreas that lets the body use sugar for energy
a chemical messenger made in the body that tells organs what to do

look.title: Treatment or Cure?
look.text: A cure makes a disease go away for good. A treatment manages a disease so a person can live well. Glasses do not cure blurry vision, but they let a person see clearly every day. Insulin works in a similar way for type 1 diabetes.
look.prompt: Is insulin a cure or a treatment? Use the glasses example to explain your answer.

check.q: Where was insulin first used to treat a patient in 1922?
check.why: The insulin work took place at the University of Toronto, where Leonard Thompson was treated in 1922.

check.q: What happens in type 1 diabetes?
choices: The pancreas does not make enough insulin
check.why: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas stops making enough insulin to use sugar for energy.

check.q: Why is insulin called a treatment and not a cure?
choices: It makes diabetes go away forever
People need it every day to manage diabetes
check.why: Insulin manages diabetes when taken regularly, but it does not make the condition go away.

lessons.title: Fleming's Discovery
lessons.mainIdea: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold made a substance, penicillin, that stopped bacteria from growing.
reading: Before antibiotics, a small cut, a sore throat or an ear infection could turn deadly if bacteria spread. Doctors had few ways to stop an infection once it began. Pneumonia, a lung infection, killed many adults and children.

In 1928, Alexander Fleming found a clear ring around a mold in a dish of bacteria. The mold was a kind of Penicillium. Its juice stopped many bacteria from growing. Fleming called the substance *penicillin*. It was the first *antibiotic* of its kind: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing.

Antibiotics work on bacteria. They do not work on viruses, such as the viruses that cause colds and flu. That is why a doctor may not give antibiotics for a cold. Taking the right medicine for the right germ, as a doctor directs, matters.

words.d: a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing; it does not work on viruses
an antibiotic first found in a mold by Alexander Fleming in 1928
a tiny germ, much smaller than bacteria, that causes illnesses such as colds and flu

look.title: Fleming's Report
look.text: Fleming reported that a mold growing on a dish of bacteria had made the colonies around it fade away, and that broth from the mold could stop the growth of many kinds of bacteria.
look.cite: Alexander Fleming, On the Antibacterial Action of Cultures of a Penicillium, British Journal of Experimental Pathology, 1929
look.prompt: What did Fleming observe, and what test did he do next to learn more?

check.q: What did Fleming notice around the mold on his dish?
choices: A clear ring where bacteria did not grow
A thick layer of extra bacteria
A crack like a broken bone
check.why: Fleming saw a clear ring around the mold where bacteria had not grown.

check.q: Which illness will antibiotics NOT treat?
choices: A cold caused by a virus
check.why: Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses such as those that cause colds.

check.q: What is an antibiotic?
choices: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth
check.why: An antibiotic kills bacteria or stops them from growing.

lessons.title: Penicillin Goes to War
lessons.mainIdea: During World War II, scientists in Britain and the United States learned to make penicillin in huge amounts.
reading: For about ten years, penicillin stayed a curiosity. It was hard to make and hard to purify. Around 1939, a team at Oxford University in England, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, with Norman Heatley, began to purify it and test it. In mice, it stopped deadly infections. Early patients improved.

World War II made the need urgent, because wounded soldiers often died of infection. Florey and Heatley flew to the United States in 1941 for help. At a government lab in Peoria, Illinois, scientists grew the mold in large tanks. A mold found on a cantaloupe from a Peoria market turned out to make much more penicillin.

Drug companies scaled up *mass production*. By the D-Day landings in 1944, large supplies were ready for Allied troops. After the war, penicillin became common for everyone. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

words.d: making a product in very large amounts, often in factories
to separate a substance from everything mixed with it

look.title: From Dish to Factory
look.text: Step 1: a scientist notices a mold in a dish. Step 2: a team purifies the substance and tests it on mice. Step 3: doctors try it on a few patients. Step 4: labs find a better mold and grow it in huge tanks. Step 5: factories make enough for millions.
look.prompt: Which step do you think was hardest? Why did it take many people, not one, to bring penicillin to patients?

check.q: Which Illinois city helped with penicillin production?
check.why: A government lab in Peoria grew the mold in tanks, and a mold from a Peoria market cantaloupe made much more penicillin.

check.q: Why did World War II make penicillin urgent?
choices: Wounded soldiers often died of infection
check.why: Many wounded soldiers died from infected wounds, so large supplies of penicillin were needed.

check.q: Who led the Oxford team that purified penicillin?
check.why: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, with Norman Heatley, purified and tested penicillin at Oxford.

lessons.title: When Bacteria Fight Back
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, so these medicines must be used only when needed and as directed.
reading: Bacteria reproduce very fast. When an antibiotic is used, most of the bacteria die. But a few may have a small change that lets them survive. Those survivors multiply. Over time, a whole population of bacteria can become hard to kill. This is *antibiotic resistance*.

Fleming warned about this in his Nobel lecture in 1945. He saw that using too little penicillin could help bacteria learn to resist it. Today, some infections, such as certain staph infections called MRSA, do not respond to common antibiotics. Doctors must use stronger or different medicines.

Everyone can help. Use antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them. Take them exactly as directed. Never share them or use old leftovers. Do not expect antibiotics for a cold. Good handwashing and vaccines also help, because fewer infections mean fewer antibiotics are needed.

words.d: when bacteria change so that an antibiotic no longer kills them
when a doctor officially orders a medicine for a patient

look.title: The Survivors
look.text: Picture a dish with 1,000 bacteria. An antibiotic kills 999. One has a small change that lets it survive. By next week, it has made millions of copies, and every copy carries the same change.
look.prompt: Will the same antibiotic work on the new millions? Explain how resistance grows.

check.q: What is antibiotic resistance?
choices: Bacteria changing so an antibiotic no longer kills them
check.why: Resistance means bacteria have changed so an antibiotic no longer works against them.

check.q: Who warned about resistance in 1945?
check.why: Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse of penicillin could let bacteria resist it.

check.q: Which habit helps slow resistance?
choices: Taking antibiotics only as a doctor directs
Asking for antibiotics for every cold
check.why: Using antibiotics only when prescribed and as directed helps slow resistance.

lessons.title: Salk's Polio Vaccine
lessons.mainIdea: In 1955 Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe and effective, and polio cases in the U.S. soon fell sharply.
reading: In the early 1950s, summer brought fear to American families. *Polio*, a disease caused by a virus, could weaken muscles, sometimes for life. Some people needed a machine called an iron lung to breathe. Pools and movie theaters sometimes closed. The worst year in the United States was 1952.

Jonas Salk, a scientist at the University of Pittsburgh, made a vaccine from polio virus that had been killed. In 1954, more than a million children took part in a huge test, called a *field trial*. On April 12, 1955, researchers announced that the vaccine was safe and worked well.

Vaccination began right away. Salk did not patent the vaccine. Later, Albert Sabin made a vaccine taken by mouth. Cases in the United States dropped quickly. Today polio has been eliminated from most of the world, and vaccination continues.

words.d: a disease caused by a virus that can weaken or paralyze muscles; prevented by vaccine
a large test of a medicine or vaccine in many people, compared with a group who did not get it

look.title: Polio Cases in the United States
look.cite: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, national polio surveillance data (rounded)
look.prompt: About how many times fewer cases were there in 1965 than in 1952? What changed in between?

check.q: What kind of vaccine did Jonas Salk make?
choices: A vaccine made from killed polio virus
check.why: Salk's vaccine used polio virus that had been killed.

check.q: What happened on April 12, 1955?
choices: Researchers announced the polio vaccine was safe and worked
Insulin was given to a boy
check.why: On April 12, 1955, the results of the field trial were announced.

check.q: Why was the 1954 field trial important?
choices: It found the polio virus under a microscope
It built the first iron lung
It tested the vaccine in more than a million children
check.why: The field trial tested the vaccine on a very large group to show it was safe and effective.

lessons.title: The Shape of DNA
lessons.mainIdea: In 1953 scientists worked out that DNA is a double helix, which explains how living things pass on instructions.
reading: Every living cell carries instructions for how to grow and work. Those instructions are stored in *DNA*. By the 1950s, scientists knew DNA was important, but not what it looked like.

In London, Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to take very sharp pictures of DNA. One image, called Photo 51, showed an X-shaped pattern. Maurice Wilkins, who worked in the same lab, showed it to James Watson. In Cambridge, Watson and Francis Crick used it and other data to build a model. In 1953 they published it: a *double helix*, like a twisted ladder.

The shape explained how DNA copies itself. The two sides unzip, and each side builds a new partner. Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize is not given after death. Many historians now stress that her work was key.

words.d: the molecule in cells that carries the instructions for how a living thing grows and works
the shape of DNA: two strands twisted around each other, like a twisted ladder

look.title: The Twisted Ladder
look.text: Picture a ladder. Now twist it gently so it spirals. The two long sides are the backbones of DNA. The rungs are pairs of chemical letters. When the ladder splits down the middle, each half can build a matching new half.
look.prompt: Why would a shape that can split and rebuild be useful for a cell that divides into two cells?

check.q: Whose X-ray photo helped reveal the shape of DNA?
check.why: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image, Photo 51, helped Watson and Crick build their model.

check.q: What shape is DNA?
choices: A double helix, like a twisted ladder
check.why: In 1953 Watson and Crick described DNA as a double helix.

check.q: Why did Franklin not share the 1962 Nobel Prize?
choices: She worked in medicine, not science
She had died, and the prize is not given after death
check.why: Franklin died in 1958, and the Nobel Prize is not awarded after death.

lessons.title: Clean Water and Sewers
lessons.mainIdea: Clean drinking water and sewers prevented huge numbers of deaths from diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
reading: Germ theory showed that dirty water spreads disease. Cities acted on that knowledge. They built sewers to carry waste away and treated drinking water to kill germs. Adding chlorine to drinking water began in the United States in the early 1900s. Cases of typhoid, another disease spread by dirty water, fell sharply.

Chicago faced a special problem. The city took its drinking water from Lake Michigan, and its sewage flowed into the Chicago River and then into the lake. In 1900 the city opened the Sanitary and Ship Canal, which reversed the river's flow so sewage moved away from the lake.

This kind of work is *public health*: protecting the health of whole communities, not just treating one patient at a time. Clean water, safe waste removal and *sanitation* may be the biggest life-savers of the 1900s. Many places in the world are still building these systems today.

words.d: work that protects the health of whole communities, such as clean water and vaccines
safe removal of sewage and waste to keep germs away from people
a serious illness caused by bacteria spread through dirty water or food

look.title: One Doctor or One Pipe?
look.text: A doctor can treat one sick child at a time. A clean water pipe reaches every home on the street, every day, before anyone gets sick.
look.prompt: Which one do you think saves more lives over many years? Explain using the idea of public health.

check.q: What did Chicago's Sanitary and Ship Canal do in 1900?
choices: Brought ocean water to the city
Reversed the river so sewage moved away from Lake Michigan
check.why: The canal reversed the Chicago River's flow to keep sewage out of the lake, the city's drinking water.

check.q: What is public health?
choices: Protecting the health of whole communities
Health care only for rich families
check.why: Public health protects whole communities, for example through clean water and vaccines.

check.q: Which disease fell sharply when cities treated drinking water?
check.why: Typhoid spreads through dirty water, so chlorinated water made cases fall.

lessons.title: Safe Food and Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: In 1906 the United States passed its first national food and drug safety laws after reports about unsafe food.
reading: In the early 1900s, some food sold in the United States was spoiled or mislabeled. Some medicines made false promises and did not list what was in them. In 1906 the writer Upton Sinclair published a novel, The Jungle, set in Chicago's meatpacking plants. It described filthy conditions, and readers were shocked.

That same year, Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act. For the first time, the national government checked meat and required truthful labels on food and medicine. This work grew into today's *Food and Drug Administration*, or FDA.

*Food safety* also means habits at home. Pasteurized milk, refrigerators, washing hands and cooking meat all the way through help keep germs out. When people read a label, check a date or keep leftovers cold, they are using ideas that grew out of germ theory.

words.d: ways of handling, cooking and storing food to prevent illness
the U.S. government agency, called the FDA, that checks the safety of food and medicines

look.title: The Pure Food and Drug Act
look.text: The law made it illegal to make or sell food, drinks or medicines that were impure or falsely labeled, and it required certain ingredients to be listed on the label.
look.cite: Pure Food and Drug Act, United States Congress, 1906
look.prompt: How does a truthful label help a family stay safe? Give one example.

check.q: Which book about Chicago meatpacking helped lead to food safety laws?
choices: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera
check.why: Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel The Jungle described filthy conditions in Chicago meatpacking plants.

check.q: What did the 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act require?
choices: Truthful labels on food and medicine
check.why: The law banned impure or falsely labeled food and medicine.

check.q: Which is a food safety habit at home?
choices: Eating meat that is still raw inside
check.why: Keeping food cold slows germ growth; the other choices raise the risk of illness.

lessons.title: How Life Expectancy Rose
lessons.mainIdea: Life expectancy in the U.S. rose by about thirty years during the 1900s, mostly because fewer children died young.
reading: *Life expectancy* is the average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live. In the United States in 1900, it was about 47 years. By 2000, it was about 77. That is a rise of about thirty years in one century.

This does not mean most adults in 1900 died at 47. Many lived into their 60s and 70s. The average was low because so many babies and young children died of infections, such as diarrhea from dirty water or milk, measles and pneumonia. When fewer children die, the average rises a lot.

What caused the rise? Clean water, sewers and safe food came first. Then vaccines and antibiotics. Better nutrition, housing and medical care also helped. Scientists still discuss how much each one added, but most agree that public health played a very large part.

words.d: the average number of years a newborn is expected to live
a single number that sums up a group, found by adding values and dividing by how many there are

look.title: U.S. Life Expectancy at Birth
look.cite: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Health Statistics, Health, United States (rounded)
look.prompt: In which 25-year period did life expectancy rise the most? Which discoveries from this chapter came during that time?

check.q: About what was U.S. life expectancy in 1900?
check.why: U.S. life expectancy at birth was about 47 years in 1900.

check.q: Why was the average so low in 1900?
choices: Many babies and young children died of infections
check.why: Many children died young from infections, which pulled the average down.

check.q: What do most scientists agree played a very large part in the rise?
choices: Public health, such as clean water and safe food
check.why: Clean water, sewers and safe food, the work of public health, played a very large part.

review.q: What did Fleming notice on his dish in 1928?
choices: Bacteria did not grow around a mold
review.why: Fleming saw a clear ring around the mold where bacteria had not grown.
Jonas Salk developed the killed-virus polio vaccine announced in 1955.

review.q: Why won't antibiotics help a cold?
choices: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work on bacteria
Colds are too mild to treat
review.why: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on the viruses that cause colds.

review.q: What role did Peoria, Illinois, play in medical history?
choices: The first X-ray was taken there
A lab there helped mass-produce penicillin
review.why: A government lab in Peoria grew penicillin mold in tanks and found a high-yield mold on a cantaloupe.

review.q: How are insulin and penicillin different?
choices: Insulin manages diabetes daily; penicillin kills bacteria in an infection
Insulin kills bacteria; penicillin controls blood sugar
review.why: Insulin is a hormone that manages diabetes; penicillin is an antibiotic against bacteria.

review.q: What did Chicago do in 1900 to protect its drinking water?
review.why: The Sanitary and Ship Canal reversed the river so sewage flowed away from the lake.

review.q: What does the rise in U.S. life expectancy from about 47 to about 77 mostly reflect?
choices: Far fewer children dying of infections
review.why: Most of the rise came because fewer babies and children died young.

review.q: How can people help slow antibiotic resistance?
choices: Take antibiotics only as a doctor prescribes
review.why: Using antibiotics only when prescribed and exactly as directed slows resistance.
